The Iranian Maritime Cyber Threat and the Changing Nature of International Conflict
item.description:
U.S. authorities are investigating whether Iran was behind a wave of suspected cyberattacks on commercial shipping, The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday. As many as 50 vessels carrying oil, liquefied petroleum and other hazardous cargoes may have been targeted. The investigation raises the prospect that the war with Iran could disrupt shipping and ports far beyond the Middle East.

The threat has been building for years. Iran-linked cyber activity has targeted shipping companies, ports and logistics firms, and the latest incidents raise the question of whether Tehran is now moving toward more disruptive and aggressive cyber operations.

The Cipher Brief spoke with Norm Roule, the former U.S. national intelligence manager for Iran, about how Tehran’s maritime cyber capabilities have evolved, what the latest investigation could mean for commercial shipping, and whether the term “gray zone” still captures the kinds of attacks governments and businesses now face.

The Cipher Brief: Should the latest report of Iranian cyberattacks against international shipping come as a surprise?

Roule: The reports are troubling, but the news won’t surprise policymakers or the shipping industry. There is a substantial body of reporting on Iranian cyber threats to international shipping dating back at least to 2019.

The Cipher Brief: When did we first see evidence of Iranian interest in operations to damage or offensively manipulate ships?

Roule: First, we should remember that as recently as August of this year, the U.S. Coast Guard and Federal Bureau of Investigation were investigating possible Iranian involvement in cyber incidents affecting two energy tankers, the VL Prosperity and the Kohaku, traveling toward the United States. It’s hard not to hear the echo of this earlier episode in the latest report.

There is considerable evidence that Iran has integrated cyber and electronic warfare capabilities into its maritime operations. In July 2019, the British-flagged Stena Impero and Liberian-flagged Mesdar reportedly experienced GPS interference before being intercepted by Iranian forces. The U.S. Maritime Administration subsequently warned shippers in the region to expect GPS interference, bridge-to-bridge communications spoofing, or other malign communications jamming with little to no warning.

By 2020, Western cybersecurity specialists and intelligence sources identified Iranian interest not merely in collecting intelligence on commercial shipping but in developing the capability to inflict physical damage on vessels. We then saw reporting that documented Iranian targeting of shipping companies, port facilities, satellite communications, logistics companies, and industrial control systems.

In July 2021, Sky News reported on leaked documents allegedly produced by Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit associated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The documents described Iranian interest in cyber operations against civilian infrastructure, vulnerabilities in maritime satellite communications, and even the possibility of sinking commercial vessels.

Later that year, Microsoft's Threat Intelligence Center reported that an Iran-linked cyber group had targeted more than 250 organizations across several strategically important sectors. Although fewer than 20 were compromised, the target list was significant. It included Persian Gulf ports, international maritime transportation companies, cargo transportation businesses, satellite imagery providers, and American and Israeli defense companies.

Microsoft assessed that the campaign supported Iranian government efforts to monitor adversary security organizations and commercial shipping and to improve Tehran's contingency planning. Of particular significance was the apparent Iranian interest in obtaining proprietary shipping records and commercial satellite imagery.

The Cipher Brief: Can you provide examples of past Iranian operations against maritime interests?

Roule: Cyber activity assessed to originate with Iran targeted Egyptian shipping and marine services companies beginning in July 2022. In May 2023, a likely Iranian actor targeted Israeli commercial websites, including those of shipping and logistics companies. The Egyptian case is particularly noteworthy because it illustrates that Iranian maritime intelligence interests were not confined to American or Israeli targets.

The Cipher Brief: What action has the United States taken against the Iranian officials responsible for developing these capabilities?

Roule: In February 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned six senior officials of the IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command for activities targeting critical infrastructure in the United States and other countries. Among those sanctioned was Hamid Reza Lashgarian, the same individual identified in the 2021 Sky News report as overseeing the Iranian cyber intelligence group associated with research into maritime vulnerabilities. Treasury confirmed that Lashgarian headed the IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command and was also a commander in the Qods Force.

The Cipher Brief: Has Iranian shipping itself been the victim of significant cyberattacks?

Roule: I can think of a couple of cases, although there may be others. In two major cyberattacks in 2025, the anti-regime hacktivist group Lab Dookhtegan, or "Sewn Lips," claimed to have disrupted satellite communications across more than 100 vessels operated by Iran's two largest state-linked shipping companies.

The group reportedly compromised an Iranian telecommunications provider, disrupting ship-to-shore communications and tracking systems on vessels belonging to the National Iranian Tanker Company and the Islamic Republic of Iran Shipping Lines. The first operation, in March 2025, reportedly affected 116 Iranian vessels. A second operation in August reportedly affected 64 ships. Taken together, these incidents appear to represent some of the most extensive cyber disruptions experienced by Iran's maritime sector.

The Cipher Brief: How has Iran's maritime cyber program evolved, and why is it so important to Tehran?

Roule: Iran's maritime cyber activities appear to have evolved in phases. Tehran's integration of cyber and electronic warfare tools into its regional maritime operations was evident by 2019. Iran subsequently increased its focus on shipping companies, port networks, satellite communications, and logistics businesses for intelligence collection and wartime contingency planning.

If confirmed, the latest suspected attacks against infrastructure and commercial vessels would show that Iran has moved to more disruptive maritime capabilities as part of a global coercion campaign. Notably, Iranian targeting has long extended beyond American and Israeli interests.

As to why the program is so important to Iran, Tehran has long understood that its ability to project power would depend heavily on asymmetric tools. Maritime cyber operations offer Tehran a means to circumvent Western naval superiority and compensate for its lack of a blue-water navy or overseas military bases. In this way, Iran can extend its maritime coercion and influence over the global economy well beyond the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb.

Also, Iran does not need to sink a ship to achieve a significant strategic effect. The propaganda value of even a failed attack can be substantial. It signals Iranian intent and geographic reach while raising questions about the effectiveness of Western deterrence. Tehran likely calculates that, whether successful or not, such operations can have economic consequences, including higher maritime insurance premiums, precautionary port closures, shipping delays, additional vessel inspections, supply chain disruptions, and increased expenditures on cybersecurity and maritime security. Iran presumably hopes that these costs will translate into domestic economic and political pressure on governments confronting Tehran.

The Cipher Brief: Could a cyberattack cause a vessel to collide with a bridge, run aground, or suffer a catastrophic explosion?

Roule: Most experts believe this is unlikely, but U.S. government authorities have explicitly identified such scenarios as credible maritime security risks.

Following the 2024 incident in Baltimore that caused the collapse of a major bridge, the U.S. government examined the potential consequences of cyber operations targeting commercial vessels. Although the Baltimore incident itself was not a cyberattack, American authorities recognized that a successful cyberattack against a large vessel's operational technology could potentially produce comparable consequences.

Whatever the nature of the incident, the implications of a cyber-induced disaster involving large commercial vessels are profound, given the cargoes they carry and their proximity to major population centers and critical infrastructure.

A significant maritime cyber incident involving an energy or chemical tanker could have enormous environmental, economic, and public safety consequences. Near a major population center, such an incident could also produce long-term public health consequences. The broader economic and homeland security implications would also be significant. Finally, American and allied maritime infrastructure is essential to U.S. military mobilization, sustainment, and overseas power projection.

The Cipher Brief: Are we doing enough to address this threat?

Roule: Likely not, but that doesn’t mean the situation has been ignored. Much of the emphasis thus far has understandably been on improving the cyber defenses of the shipping industry and general security management of related architecture.

There is no public evidence that Iran has successfully conducted a destructive cyberattack against a commercial vessel on the high seas. It would nevertheless be imprudent to assume that Tehran will not seek to develop these capabilities or use artificial intelligence to produce such tools more quickly.

We can also say that the international community has not established credible deterrence against Iran and other countries deploying these tools. Unfortunately, sanctions alone will not be sufficient to prevent their employment. A meaningful threat of military action will likely be required.

The Cipher Brief: What does Iran's development of these capabilities tell us about the changing nature of international power projection?

Roule: We are watching the nature of international power projection change in real time.

Iran's activities should reinforce concerns that the instruments employed in regional conflicts will increasingly be deployed globally, even when conventional military operations remain geographically concentrated. The consequences are profound. Iran is showing that adversaries with limited conventional expeditionary military capabilities can potentially threaten commercial infrastructure thousands of miles from their territory and impose high costs on adversaries possessing overwhelming conventional military superiority.

Other adversaries are watching how this conflict plays out. Middle powers willing to engage in such activities will increasingly seek to achieve the sort of strategic disruption previously associated primarily with major military and intelligence powers.

This is not to suggest that conventional military power has lost its importance. Rather, it is to recognize that neither conventional military superiority nor geographic distance provides the same degree of protection against hostile operations on one's own territory that it once did.

The Cipher Brief: Iran is hardly alone in this respect. How do its activities compare with what we have seen from Russia?

Roule: Russia's activities have been particularly consequential, and there is little reason to believe that Tehran has not studied both the nature of Russian operations and the international response to them. Moscow has been blamed for many cyber incidents, so I will only cite a few.

In 2022, a Russian cyberattack against the Viasat satellite communications network disrupted communications and affected European wind energy infrastructure. Since then, numerous operations attributed to Moscow have sought to interfere with satellite navigation systems supporting civilian aviation and maritime transportation. France also publicly attributed cyber operations against its interests to Russia in 2025.

These activities occurred alongside actual or suspected Russian external operations involving arson against a British warehouse containing equipment destined for Ukraine, sabotage targeting international air freight networks, underwater telecommunications and energy infrastructure, railway infrastructure, drone incidents affecting European airports, and attacks against commercial vessels in the Black Sea.

It is difficult to imagine that Tehran has not taken note of the feeble international response to these activities when considering its own offensive cyber operations, threats against dissidents and journalists abroad, and provision of missile and drone technology to the Houthis and other proxies.

The Cipher Brief: Has Ukraine's response to Russian aggression also demonstrated the changing geographic boundaries of warfare?

Roule: Ukraine is certainly not the moral equivalent of Russia or Iran. But in its valiant fight against Moscow, it has demonstrated that a middle power confronting a conventionally superior adversary can extend the geographic scope of conflict well beyond the principal theater of military operations.

The alleged Ukrainian involvement in the September 2022 destruction of the Nord Stream pipelines, the 2025 operations against Russian-linked vessels in the Black Sea and Mediterranean, and attacks against Russian offshore oil infrastructure illustrate the expanding geographic reach of the conflict.

More recent Ukrainian drone operations, including the November attack at Benghazi, Libya, on the Russian corvette Merkury, which sank, and the cargo vessel Angara, together with strikes on a Russian corvette and a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland, further demonstrate the ability of a country with limited conventional expeditionary capabilities to threaten its adversary's interests across multiple theaters.

The strategic lesson is that countries geographically distant from a conflict may nonetheless find themselves, their territorial waters, or their commercial infrastructure drawn into its battlespace with little notice. A conflict that might once have been regarded as regional can now generate security consequences across several continents.

The Cipher Brief: What do these developments tell us about the changing nature of warfare?

Roule: We are at a remarkable moment in modern military history, but we should be cautious about suggesting that we fully understand where these developments will lead. However, certain trends are clear.

First, Iran's actions in the Middle East illustrate how modern conflicts increasingly unfold along an unpredictable, prolonged, and multi-theater continuum rather than through clearly defined periods of war and peace. Hostile governments may regard themselves as engaged in a sustained confrontation even when Western governments consider themselves to be at peace. Espionage, influence operations, sabotage, intimidation, political interference, and even overt military operations can occur routinely, simultaneously, and often in plain sight.

Next, the geographic boundaries of a conflict are becoming increasingly porous, making the traditional distinction between the front line and the rear area less meaningful. A war in Ukraine could lead to sabotage in England, Germany, and the Baltic Sea. A conflict involving Iran can generate assassination plots in the United States, cyberattacks in Europe, and threats against shipping in multiple oceans that undermine the economies of distant countries. A future conflict over Taiwan could involve the disruption of civilian infrastructure in continental North America.

Finally, countries that are not direct military participants in a conflict may nevertheless experience its economic, security, and physical consequences without being able to stop the aggressor from repeating its attacks.

The Cipher Brief: How does this change the security calculations of governments and commercial enterprises?

Roule: Several points come to mind.

Countries are learning that defenders must protect a vast network of facilities and commercial activities, while adversaries can concentrate their limited resources on selected objectives. As shippers in the Gulf will likely agree, companies are learning that protection by the international community against open aggression is neither guaranteed nor complete.

Governments and corporations must now recognize that relatively inexpensive hostile operations can compel them to make substantial investments in security, redundancy, intelligence collection, and infrastructure protection. An adversary need not destroy a commercial facility to make its operation more expensive, politically controversial, or commercially unattractive.

Commercial and civilian infrastructure will remain a strategic center of gravity in future conflicts. The distinction between commercial security and national security will become increasingly difficult to sustain.

The Cipher Brief: Is the term "gray-zone conflict" still adequate to describe what we are witnessing?

Roule: Increasingly, the terminology seems insufficient to convey the open intensity of the actions being undertaken. Its continued use may even be softening perceptions of the violence involved.

The phrase is useful when describing coercive activities deliberately calibrated to avoid conventional warfare. However, there is nothing inherently gray about Iranian attacks against commercial shipping, drone attacks against vessels and airports, cyber operations intended to destroy civilian infrastructure, or terrorism conducted on the territory of another country.

Is this terrorism? War? What is it? The distinction between wartime and peacetime has been eroding for years as clever aggressors exploit how the world has come to recognize and deal with aggression.

Russia, Iran, and China have demonstrated that geography, conventional military inferiority, and the absence of an expeditionary military capability no longer prevent a state from imposing high costs on distant adversaries or deterring significant retaliation. Their power comes less from their military strength and more from making critical economic arteries, commercial infrastructure, and the homeland itself operational theaters.

Unfortunately, the term "gray zone" increasingly describes the uncertainty, political hesitation, or diplomatic indecision of the defender rather than the character of the aggressor's campaign.

Consider Iran's reported daily attacks against civilian shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf. Not since the Tanker War of the 1980s, when Iran and Iraq attacked hundreds of merchant ships, have civilian vessels from so many countries, carrying cargoes so important to the economies of so many others, been subjected to sustained attack by a state asserting authority over international navigation that it has no legitimate basis to exercise. More than two dozen mariners have been killed and many others injured. The dead include citizens of India, Thailand, and the Philippines.

The weak international response is not an isolated case. Iranian and Houthi attacks against civilian targets during the past decade elicited a similarly limited global response despite leaving dead and wounded from many countries. A reported Iranian drone plot against a Royal Air Force base in England and disrupted terrorist operations in France and the United States have also failed to produce a publicly evident deterrent effect sufficient to end such activities, even though a successful attack could well have caused multiple casualties.

While the barriers to conducting such operations have declined, the threshold for a direct conventional or even unconventional response by the victim remains extraordinarily high. This remarkable disparity provides a tremendous advantage to adversaries. Policymakers have understandably been reluctant to establish firm red lines that might constrain their freedom of action. But in the absence of credible consequences, Iran and its proxies have little incentive to refrain from employing these capabilities to their fullest extent, placing the citizens and commercial interests of numerous countries at risk.

The Cipher Brief: Looking ahead three to five years, where are these trends likely to take us?

Roule: Recognizing that my crystal ball is no better than that of any of your readers, it seems highly likely that Western countries will see more frequent attacks against civilian infrastructure, greater geographic expansion of regional conflicts, increased state use of organized crime, and higher structural costs for international commerce. Geographic distance, neutrality, and the absence of direct military involvement in a conflict will provide diminishing protection against its consequences.

Russia, Iran, and other revisionist and aggressor countries will increasingly employ criminal intermediaries to conduct hostile operations, complicating attribution, counterintelligence, and diplomatic responses. Middle powers, observing the strategic utility and relatively limited penalties associated with these operations, will expand their cyber, intelligence, unmanned systems, and covert-action capabilities. Repeated violations of territorial sovereignty without meaningful consequences will further erode international norms, with particularly serious implications for smaller states.

The economic and domestic security consequences will be substantial. Shipping, aviation, energy, telecommunications, and financial companies will face increased expenditures on physical security, cybersecurity, insurance, infrastructure redundancy, regulatory compliance, and operational recovery. These costs will increasingly constitute a permanent geopolitical risk premium rather than a temporary wartime expense.

Commercial enterprises will be exposed to geopolitical pressures stemming from the nationality of their owners, customers, cargoes, or trading partners. Western governments will devote greater resources to counterintelligence, counterterrorism, infrastructure protection, and counter-drone capabilities, while requiring private industry to assume greater responsibility for risks historically regarded as matters of national defense.

The Cipher Brief: We have covered a lot of ground. How would you summarize the current situation in closing?

Roule: The international community is witnessing the accelerating evolution in which states increasingly possess the means and willingness to conduct persistent and potentially lethal operations against distant adversaries without deploying conventional military forces or declaring war. This ability to project disruptive and coercive power is proliferating more rapidly than governments' ability or willingness to deter its use.

Conventional military superiority is no longer sufficient to guarantee territorial security. Middle powers, smaller states, and even non-state organizations have acquired instruments capable of imposing substantial economic and security costs on much larger powers. Wars will likely remain geographically concentrated, but their instruments and consequences will become increasingly global. This dynamic inherently involves strategies the mean civilian infrastructure and international commerce will be increasingly common elements of interstate conflict.

The principal danger remains not that every hostile operation will cause catastrophic damage. It is that the international system is increasingly normalizing a level of interstate violence and coercion that would previously have constituted a major international crisis and produced coalitions to confront aggressors and preserve the international order.

item.title: Democratic voters want Congress to cut funding for Iran war: polls
item.description:
Democratic voters want Congress to quickly cut off funding for the Iran war and are prepared to punish lawmakers who fail to do so, two new polls suggest.

With government funding set to expire on December 11, congressional Democrats are weighing whether to withhold their support for any spending bill unless it includes restrictions on funding for the war. Such a move would leave Trump and congressional supporters of the conflict to decide whether to accept those restrictions or risk a government shutdown to keep the war going. The new polling indicates that pursuing this strategy would have considerable support among the Democratic party’s base.

Opposition to the Iran war helped fuel Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories earlier this month. Now, the question of how quickly the party should move to end the conflict has become a dividing line for the party, including in the race for Senate majority leader. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) has made the December 11 war funding deadline a key plank of his bid to unseat Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as party leader.

A University of Maryland poll released Tuesday shows that 80% of Democratic respondents want the Iran war to end “now, regardless of the terms.” Only 14% said they would prefer to stay the course until Iran offered concessions, and 3% wanted to escalate “in an attempt to force Iran to accept US terms.” Exactly one-quarter of Republicans and 59% of independents agreed with the majority of Democrats that the war should end now.

Respondents were more split over the specifics of whether to include a cut-off for funding in a stopgap funding bill. Just over half of Democrats (51%) said they would favor such a strategy, even at the risk of a veto and potential shutdown. A mere 16% said they were opposed to the maneuver. Across all respondents, 31% supported including language to cut funding, 28% opposed, and 39% replied “don’t know.”

“As is implicit in the wording of our poll question on this issue, the Democratic public is apparently prepared to take that risk [of a shutdown],” the University of Maryland’s Shibley Telhami wrote in his accompanying analysis of the shutdown question. “On the other hand, Trump may be looking for a way to end the war, and cutting war funding may provide him with an exit ramp, while blaming Congress, especially Democrats, for the consequences.”

On Wednesday, progressive group Demand Progress released a new poll that digs further into the question of the political consequences if such a vote were to take place.

According to the poll, just over three-quarters (76%) of respondents who voted for Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in 2024 said they would be “less likely to reelect a lawmaker who votes to extend government funding past December 11 without a ban on funding for the war against Iran.” Nearly half of Harris voters said they would be “much less likely” to support a member who voted to keep funding the war, and only 7% said they would be “much” or “somewhat” more likely to vote for someone who supported legislation that did not cut funds.

Even among voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024, only 38% said they would be more likely to reelect a lawmaker who voted to extend government funding without prohibiting further money for the war. A plurality of respondents (29%) said that it would have no impact, while 19% said that they would be less likely to support a member of Congress who supported such a bill.

The Demand Progress poll surveyed 1,006 voters from November 18 to November 20.

Many Democratic skeptics of including Iran-funding-specific provisions in future funding bills have pointed to the potential political costs of being blamed for a government shutdown as a reason to avoid such a debate during the lame duck period.

But among the party’s own voters, there may also be a political price to pay for waiting.

item.title: Iraq's top court says Baghdad can deploy troops to secure borders in Kurdistan region
item.description:
By Muayad Hameed and Tala Ramadan

BAGHDAD, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Iraq's highest court ruled on Wednesday that Baghdad can deploy federal forces along all international borders, including in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region,backing Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's push to assert more central control.

Zaidi ordered federal authorities on Tuesday to take over border crossings run by the Kurdistan Regional Government, and has also demanded authority over oil fields controlled by Kurdish security forces, following a probe into smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company.

item.title: In Lebanon, the opening of a second airport reflects political shifts
item.description:
By Laila Bassam and Nazih Osseiran

KLEIAT AIRPORT, Lebanon, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Lebanon plans to open a second international airport next month to bring economic growth to the poorer north, in a project that underlines the diminished political sway of the Hezbollah group, which had long opposed it.

Kleiat Airport, located on the Mediterranean coast, about 20 km (12 miles) from the border crossing to Syria, will offer another gateway to Lebanon alongside Beirut international airport, where travel has been disrupted by wars between Israel and Hezbollah in recent years.

item.title: Israeli strike kills Hamas official, his wife and children
item.description:
By Nidal al-Mughrabi

CAIRO, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Israel's military killed a senior Hamas security official as well as his wife and two children with an airstrike on their Gaza Strip apartment early on Wednesday, Gaza's Hamas-run Interior Ministry and medics said.

The airstrike that killed Mohammad Abuelouf, a Hamas colonel who headed the militants' internal security service in northern Gaza, and his family was the second Israeli attack to kill a senior Hamas security official in the past 24 hours.

item.title: Iran says it is prepared to withstand US blockade, seeks to curb price rises
item.description:
DUBAI, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Iran's first vice president said on Wednesday Tehran was not concerned about a US naval blockade as there had been a significant increase in cargo through other borders, and that the government was seeking to rein in price rises.

Tehran is facing one of its worst inflation surges in decades, driven by the nearly nine-month-old Iran war, with a particularly sharp rise in food prices.

item.title: High spending, low impact: Can Germany’s defence policy deliver on strategic ambition – and deter Russia?
item.description:
High spending, low impact: Can Germany’s defence policy deliver on strategic ambition – and deter Russia? Expert comment jon.wallace 25 November 2026

An unpopular government must train its civil service how to deliver a strategy at a time of technological upheaval – while persuading a sceptical public. It has some resources to draw on.

The significant increase in German defence spending since 2022 has been celebrated as a success story for European security. Germany has the stated ambition to become the largest land power in Europe, with a core defence budget set to rise to 3.5 per cent of GDP by 2029.

To support this effort, some initial procurement reforms are already taking place: plans were unveiled earlier in the year to reform the defence procurement agency. But Germany still struggles with the strategic and cultural transformation across society that will be necessary to realize its ambitions.

In its political and military leadership, there is an incomplete understanding of how German deterrence is meant to work, what kind of a future conflict to expect and as a result, what systems Germany needs to acquire. That risks making the increased defence spending inefficient, undermining fragile public support for rearmament. And it could send confusing signals to industry.

The challenge is complex. And it comes at a time of technological, political and strategic upheaval. But Germany has important resources to draw on.

A clear strategy

Like many NATO allies, Germany has updated its security and defence strategic documents over the last few years. At first glance, these look comparable to those of other NATO nations. But Germany continues to struggle to translate them into action.

Part of this challenge might be that some documents, such as the Bundeswehr’s military strategy published in 2026, were produced for the first time. Other NATO countries have established pathways for turning a strategy into action, but Germany has to figure it out from scratch.

What’s more, in some cases procurement has come ahead of the strategy. That partly makes sense: Germany could not wait until 2026 to start acquiring new systems, considering the changed security environment. But it also seems to have inhibited procurement reform, sent mixed messages to industry and led to some disjointed and traditional contracts.

Examples of this include post-contract adjustments to a large order of Boxer armoured vehicles. Additionally, traditional procurement types have been prioritized to date: orders placed have tended towards big, traditional equipment – frigates, helicopters, armoured vehicles.

These are all important and the Bundeswehr needs more of them. However, in the NATO comparison, the Bundeswehr compares poorly for orders placed for uncrewed systems and digital support infrastructure.

Meanwhile, Berlin is struggling to adapt to the pace of technological change in war, and its effect on deterrence. Newer military technologies complicate old assumptions about the balance between conventional and nuclear deterrence. Some advanced conventional capabilities, such as deep precision strike, are taking on parts of a traditionally nuclear deterrence mission.

But NATO thinking since the end of the cold war created silos where nuclear and conventional capabilities were seen as entirely separate, rather than as levers of the same concept of deterrence. This means that non-nuclear allies like Germany have not invested much thought in how their militaries can deter. Conventional militaries’ role was traditionally to defend, not deter aggression or fight to win. The absence of good understanding of what to deter and what kind of fight to expect hampers German decision making when it comes to military procurement.

Germany now needs to find a way to upskill its officials and civil servants to better understand deterrence concepts, especially how to tailor deterrence according to the perceptions of its potential adversaries.

These discussions must be had across a broad spectrum of the German political and military leadership. There needs to be a consensus understanding of what Russia has learned from the war in Ukraine, how it is applying these lessons to its thinking about war with NATO, and what capability gaps Germany and other NATO countries have.

Public opinion

Germany’s security leadership also faces a domestic challenge. The German government has struggled to take the public along with its messaging on the re-armament agenda and especially support for Ukraine.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz won election on a platform that included stronger support for Ukraine. But his handling of domestic issues has seen his popularity plunge to the lowest on record for a German chancellor.

Falling support for the government is mirrored by the rise of the far-right party Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). A significant majority of its supporters oppose support for Ukraine, and its leadership does not see Russia as a threat to Germany. It would likely be a serious challenge to EU and NATO cooperation on European security were the AfD to become a party of government.

Mending fences

An additional political factor Germany has to navigate is how to define its new European security leadership role in relation to its neighbours.

Allies like Poland remain uncomfortable with the idea of Germany providing security leadership for Europe. That is especially true in the context of rising AfD support. ‘We remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,’ said Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski in September, following the AfD’s record result in the regional Saxony-Anhalt election. 

Germany and Poland will both be part of the negotiations for upcoming Ukraine peace talks. Polish negotiators will undoubtedly watch very carefully for any signs of German concessions towards Russia, as Poland has long been critical of the former German approach of prioritizing business relations with Russia.

These factors combine for a difficult burden: Germany needs to navigate internal cultural and structural reform as well as a difficult domestic landscape, while being under the scrutiny of its allies.

The way forward

Germany does have resources it can draw on. When seeking to upskill its officials in deterrence doctrine, it can learn from NATO partners’ plans: the UK also recognized it has lost deterrence knowledge across its civil service and is running regular training courses for civil servants. Germany also has a vibrant academic community specializing in strategic thinking – people who would welcome working more closely with government and delivering some of this work.

Procurement reform has been written about widely, but a simple and affordable improvement might be for the German government to be more disciplined in publishing a list of priorities for procurement, so that industry can react and compete accordingly.

Perhaps more challenging is how to better engage Germany’s neighbours. The German government has tried a range of different confidence-building measures with Poland, similar to its efforts that helped transform the relationship with France. 

However, Polish concerns about Russia and its suspicion of Germany run deep. It will take time to strengthen those relationships. Germany will also have to demonstrate that the ‘Zeitenwende’ is a real, long-term, sustained change, maintaining its current focus on security and defence. Its leading role in the NATO forward deployment, and participation in joint Baltic and Eastern flank exercises will play a significant role here.

In order to bring its people along, the German government needs to develop a sustained and coherent narrative about the risk the country faces from Russia, and all that it is doing to keep Germany safe, and German democracy strong and free. 

It will also need to improve its messaging especially for young Germans. It must highlight the opportunities it is creating for them, rather than scaring them with mixed messages on forced conscription – when they are already dissatisfied with their employment and educational opportunities.

The attacks came after the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had struck Yemen's Red Sea port city of Hodeida, drawing threats of retaliation from the Yemeni fighters.

"Both operations resulted in damage to the targeted sites," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said.
